      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Lupus</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Cutaneous <span class="qt0">Lupus</span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">SLE</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Subacute Cutaneous <span class="qt0">Lupus</span></content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt2">Systemic</span> <span class="qt0">Lupus</span> <span class="qt1">Erythematosus</span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Discoid <span class="qt0">lupus</span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt0">lupus</span>?<p><span class="qt0">Lupus</span> is a chronic (long-lasting) type of autoimmune disease. Autoimmune diseases happen when your immune system attacks healthy cells and tissues by mistake. This attack causes inflammation. It can also damage many parts of the body, including the joints, skin, kidneys, heart, lungs, and brain.</p><p>There are several types of <span class="qt0">lupus</span>:</p><ul><li><span class="qt2">Systemic</span> <span class="qt0">lupus</span> <span class="qt1">erythematosus</span> (SLE) is the most common type. It can be mild or severe and can affect many parts of the body.</li><li>Cutaneous <span class="qt0">lupus</span> affects the skin. It causes a rash or sores, usually after your skin is exposed to sunlight. The two major types of cutaneous <span class="qt0">lupus</span> are discoid <span class="qt0">lupus</span> and subacute cutaneous <span class="qt0">lupus</span>.</li><li>Drug-induced <span class="qt0">lupus</span> is caused by a reaction to some medicines. The symptoms may start 3 to 6 months after starting the medicine. The symptoms usually go away when you stop taking the medicine.</li><li>Neonatal <span class="qt0">lupus</span>, which is rare, affects newborns. It is caused by certain antibodies that are passed from the pregnant mother to the fetus.</li></ul>What causes <span class="qt0">lupus</span>?<p>The cause of <span class="qt0">lupus</span> is unknown. Researchers are studying what might cause or trigger the disease, such as:</p><ul><li>Genetics</li><li>Environmental factors, such as viral infections, sunlight, certain medicines, and smoking</li><li>Problems with the immune system</li></ul>Who is more likely to get <span class="qt0">lupus</span>?<p>Anyone can get <span class="qt0">lupus</span>, but women get it much more often than men.</p><p><span class="qt0">Lupus</span> is more common in African Americans than in White people. It is also more common in people of American Indian and Asian descent.  African American and Hispanic women are more likely to have severe forms of <span class="qt0">lupus</span>.</p>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt0">lupus</span>?<p><span class="qt0">Lupus</span> can have many symptoms, and they differ from person to person. Some of the more common ones are:</p><ul><li>Arthritis, causing painful and swollen joints and morning stiffness</li><li>Fever</li><li>Fatigue or feeling tired often</li><li>Red rash, most often on the face (also called the "butterfly rash")</li><li>Chest pain when taking a deep breath</li><li>Hair loss</li><li>Pale or purple fingers or toes, from cold and stress (Raynaud phenomenon) </li><li>Sensitivity to the sun</li><li>Swelling in legs or around eyes</li><li>Mouth ulcers</li><li>Swollen glands</li><li>Headache and dizziness</li><li>Confusion and memory problems</li></ul><p>Symptoms may come and go. When you are having symptoms, it is called a flare.  Flares can range from mild to severe. New symptoms may appear at any time.</p>What other problems can <span class="qt0">lupus</span> cause?<p><span class="qt0">Lupus</span> causes inflammation throughout your body. This can cause problems in your organs, including:</p><ul><li>Kidney damage (<span class="qt0">lupus</span> nephritis).</li><li>Heart problems, including inflammation in the heart (myocarditis), heart valves, or lining of the heart muscle (pericarditis).</li><li>Inflammation of blood vessels (vasculitis).</li><li>Blood clots</li><li>Inflammation of the tissue that surrounds the lungs (pleurisy). This can make it painful to breathe.</li></ul><p>Some people with <span class="qt0">lupus</span> may be more likely to develop other conditions, such as coronary artery disease (CAD) and atherosclerosis.</p>How is <span class="qt0">lupus</span> diagnosed?<p>There is no specific test for <span class="qt0">lupus</span>, and it's often mistaken for other diseases that cause similar symptoms. So it may take a while to get a diagnosis. To find out if you have <span class="qt0">lupus</span>, your health care provider: </p><ul><li>Will ask about your symptoms, medical history, and family health history</li><li>Will do a complete physical exam</li><li>May order blood tests, such as ANA (antinuclear antibody), antibodies, complete blood count, and complement  tests</li><li>May order other tests, such as urine tests</li><li>May do biopsies:
  <ul><li>Skin biopsy (looking at skin samples under a microscope)</li><li>Kidney biopsy (looking at tissue from your kidney under a microscope)</li></ul>
</li></ul>What are the treatments for <span class="qt0">lupus</span>?<p>There is no cure for <span class="qt0">lupus</span>, but medicines and lifestyle changes can help control it.</p><p>People with <span class="qt0">lupus</span> often need to see different providers. You will most likely have a primary care provider and a rheumatologist (a doctor who specializes in autoimmune and other diseases of the bones, joints, and muscles). Which other specialists you may need depend on how <span class="qt0">lupus</span> affects your body. For example, if <span class="qt0">lupus</span> is damaging your heart or blood vessels, you would see a cardiologist (a doctor who specializes in heart diseases).</p><p>Your primary care provider should coordinate care between all of your other providers and treat other problems as they come up. You and your primary care provider will develop a treatment plan to fit your needs. You will both review the plan often to make sure that it is working. You should report new symptoms to your provider right away so that your treatment plan can be changed, if needed.</p><p></p><p>The goals of a treatment plan are to:</p><ul><li>Prevent flares</li><li>Treat flares when they occur</li><li>Reduce organ damage and other problems</li><li>Improve your quality of life</li></ul><p>Treatments may include drugs to:</p><ul><li>Reduce fever, swelling, and pain</li><li>Reduce inflammation in your body</li><li>Prevent or reduce flares</li><li>Reduce or prevent damage to joints</li><li>Suppress (lower) the activity of your immune system</li></ul><p>Newer medicines are now available for some types of <span class="qt0">lupus</span>, including <span class="qt0">lupus</span> that affects the kidneys. These medicines work by targeting specific parts of the immune system. Besides taking medicines for <span class="qt0">lupus</span>, you may need to take medicines for problems that are related to <span class="qt0">lupus</span> such as high cholesterol, high blood pressure, or infections.</p><p>Alternative and complementary therapies are therapies that are not part of standard treatments. Some people try alternative and complementary therapies to improve their <span class="qt0">lupus</span> symptoms. But research has not clearly shown whether these treatments may help or treat <span class="qt0">lupus</span>. Talk to your provider before trying any new treatments.</p><p>Researchers are also studying treatments, such as CAR-T cell therapy, for <span class="qt0">lupus</span> that hasn't improved with other medicines. New treatments like this are usually only available by joining a research study, until they're approved for general use.</p>How can I cope with <span class="qt0">lupus</span>?<p>It is important to take an active role in your treatment. It helps to learn more about <span class="qt0">lupus</span> - being able to spot the warning signs of a flare can help you prevent the flare or make the symptoms less severe.</p><p>It is also important to find ways to cope with the stress of having <span class="qt0">lupus</span>. Exercising and finding ways to relax may make it easier for you to cope. A good support system can also help.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases</p></content>
